paragraphs: To Be Found in the United States

The first thing that strikes a traveler in the United States is the huge number of people trying to rise out of the condition they were born into. The second is how seldom one sees lofty ambition amid this restless, universal striving. Every American longs to get ahead, yet hardly any seem to cherish great hopes or to aim very high. All are constantly trying to gain property, power, and reputation, but few think of these things on a grand scale. This is all the more surprising because nothing in the customs or laws of America appears to hold desire back or to keep it from pressing outward in every direction. It seems hard to attribute this odd state of affairs to the equality of social conditions, since at the moment that same equality was established in France, ambition took flight without limit. Even so, I believe the chief cause that can be given for this fact lies in the social condition and the democratic customs of the Americans.

Every revolution enlarges men’s ambition, and this is especially true of revolutions that overthrow an aristocracy. When the old barriers that kept the multitude away from fame and power are suddenly torn down, everyone surges upward toward the heights they have coveted for so long and can at last enjoy. In this first rush of triumph nothing seems impossible to anyone. Desires are boundless, and the power to satisfy them seems almost boundless too. Laws and customs are renewed all at once, and all men and all institutions are thrown into vast confusion. Amid it, the members of the community rise and fall again with extreme speed, and power passes so quickly from hand to hand that no one need despair of seizing it in turn. We must also remember that the people who destroy an aristocracy have lived under its laws. They have seen its splendor, and without noticing it they have absorbed the feelings and ideas it held. So at the moment an aristocracy breaks up, its spirit still pervades the mass of the community, and its tendencies linger long after its defeat. Ambition therefore stays extremely great for as long as a democratic revolution lasts, and it remains so for some time after the revolution is over. Men do not forget the extraordinary events they have witnessed in a single day. The passions a revolution has stirred up do not vanish when it ends. A sense of instability lingers even in restored order. The notion that success comes easily outlives the strange reversals that produced it. Desires stay greatly inflated while the means of satisfying them shrink day by day. The taste for large fortunes persists, though large fortunes have become rare. On every side we see the ravages of excessive and unhappy ambition, kindled in hearts that it consumes in secret and to no purpose.

In the end, however, the last traces of the struggle fade away. The remnants of the aristocracy vanish completely, and people forget the great events that accompanied its fall. Peace follows war, and order rules again in the new realm. Desires are once more fitted to the means of fulfilling them. The needs, opinions, and feelings of men fall into agreement again. The level of the community is fixed for good, and democratic society is established. A democratic nation that has reached this settled and regular state of things will offer a very different sight from the one we have just described. We may readily conclude that if ambition grows great while the conditions of society are becoming equal, it loses that quality once they have become so. Wealth is divided into smaller shares and knowledge is spread widely, so no one is wholly without education or property. The privileges and disqualifications of caste are abolished, and men have broken the bonds that held them in place. The idea of advancement then occurs to every mind, the wish to rise swells in every heart, and everyone wants to climb above his station. Ambition becomes the universal feeling.

But if the equality of conditions gives every member of the community some resources, it also keeps any of them from having resources on a large scale. That necessarily confines their desires within rather narrow limits. So among democratic nations ambition is ardent and unceasing, but it does not usually aim high. Life is mostly spent in eagerly pursuing small goals that lie within reach. What chiefly turns the men of democracies away from lofty ambition is not the smallness of their fortunes but the fierceness of the efforts they make every day to improve them. They strain their faculties to the utmost to achieve paltry results, and this cannot fail to narrow their vision and limit their powers before long. They could be much poorer and still be greater. The small number of wealthy citizens found in a democracy are no exception to this rule. A man who rises gradually to wealth and power picks up, during this long labor, habits of prudence and restraint that he can never afterward shake off. A man cannot enlarge his mind the way he enlarges his house. The same applies to the sons of such a man. They are born, it is true, into a high position, but their parents were humble. They have grown up among feelings and ideas that they cannot easily get rid of later, and we may presume that they will inherit their father’s inclinations along with his wealth. The opposite may happen: the poorest descendant of a powerful aristocracy may show vast ambition, because the traditional opinions of his family and the general spirit of his order still carry him, for a time, above his means. Something else also keeps the men of democratic periods from readily pursuing lofty goals: they foresee how much time must pass before they are ready to approach them. “It is a great advantage,” says Pascal, “to be a man of quality, since it brings one man as forward at eighteen or twenty as another man would be at fifty, which is a clear gain of thirty years.” Those thirty years are usually missing for the ambitious men of democracies. The principle of equality, which lets every man arrive at everything, prevents all men from advancing quickly.

In a democratic society, as anywhere else, only a certain number of great fortunes can be made. And because the paths leading to them are open to all without distinction, everyone’s progress must be slowed. The candidates look nearly alike, and it is hard to choose among them without violating the principle of equality, which is the supreme law of democratic societies. So the first idea that occurs is to make them all advance at the same pace and go through the same trial. Thus, the more alike men become, and the more peacefully and deeply the principle of equality enters the institutions and customs of the country, the stiffer the rules of advancement grow. Advancement itself becomes slower, and it becomes far harder to reach a certain height quickly. Out of hatred of privilege, and out of the difficulty of choosing, all men are finally compelled, whatever their abilities, to pass the same ordeal. All are subjected without distinction to a host of petty preliminary exercises, in which their youth is wasted and their imagination is snuffed out. They despair of ever fully attaining what is held out to them, and by the time they are at last able to do something extraordinary, they have lost the taste for it.

In China, where equality of conditions is extreme and very ancient, no man moves from one public office to another without going through a probationary trial. This trial begins again at every stage of his career. The idea is by now so rooted in the customs of the people that I remember reading a Chinese novel in which the hero, after countless setbacks, finally wins his beloved’s heart by earning honors. Lofty ambition can hardly breathe in such an atmosphere.

What I say of politics applies to everything. Equality produces the same effects everywhere. Where a country’s laws do not regulate and slow men’s advancement by explicit enactment, competition accomplishes the same thing. In a well-established democratic community, then, great and rapid elevation is rare. It is an exception to the common rule, and the very strangeness of such cases makes men forget how seldom they occur. People living in democracies come to see this in the end. They find out that the laws of their country open a boundless field of action before them, but that no one can hope to hurry across it. Between themselves and the final object of their desires they see a multitude of small intermediate obstacles, which must be overcome slowly. This prospect wearies their ambition and discourages it at once. They therefore give up hopes so doubtful and distant, and look closer to hand for pleasures that are less lofty and easier to obtain. Their horizon is not limited by the laws; they narrow it themselves.

I have observed that lofty ambitions are rarer in ages of democracy than in aristocratic times. I may add that when they do arise in spite of these natural obstacles, their character is different. In aristocracies the career of ambition is often broad, but its boundaries are fixed. In democracies ambition usually moves within a narrower field, but once it gets beyond that field, hardly any limits can be set on it. Men are individually weak. They live apart from one another and in constant motion. Precedents carry little authority and laws last only a short time. So resistance to novelty is feeble, and the structure of society never looks fully upright or firmly consolidated. As a result, once an ambitious man has power in his grasp, there is nothing he will not dare. When power slips from him, he plots the overthrow of the state to win it back. This gives great political ambition a character of revolutionary violence that it seldom shows to the same degree in aristocratic communities. The usual picture in democratic nations is a great number of small and very reasonable objects of ambition. From among them, at intervals, a few ill-controlled desires of larger growth break out. But ambition conceived and carried out on a vast scale is not to be found there.

I have shown elsewhere by what hidden influence the principle of equality makes the passion for physical gratifications and the exclusive love of the present dominate the human heart. These propensities mix with the feeling of ambition and tinge it, so to speak, with their colors. I believe that ambitious men in democracies are less concerned than any others with the interests and the judgment of posterity. The present moment alone engages and absorbs them. They are more inclined to complete a number of undertakings quickly than to raise lasting monuments to their achievements, and they care far more for success than for fame. What they most demand from men is obedience, and what they most covet is empire. Their manners have almost always stayed below the height of their station. The result is that they often bring very low tastes into their extraordinary fortunes, and they seem to have acquired supreme power only to serve their coarse or petty pleasures.

I think that in our time it is very necessary to purify, regulate, and adapt the feeling of ambition, but that it would be extremely dangerous to try to impoverish it or suppress it too much. We should try to set certain outer limits that it must never be allowed to cross, but within those limits its range should not be restricted too far. I admit that what I fear for democratic society is not so much the boldness of desires as their mediocrity. What seems to me most to be dreaded is that, amid the small and ceaseless occupations of private life, ambition may lose its vigor and its greatness. I fear that the passions of man may subside and at the same time be lowered, so that the march of society becomes every day calmer and less aspiring. I think, then, that the leaders of modern society would be wrong to try to lull the community with a state of happiness that is too uniform and too peaceful. It is good to expose the community from time to time to difficulty and danger, in order to raise ambition and give it a field of action. Moralists constantly complain that the ruling vice of the present time is pride. This is true in one sense, for no one thinks he is not better than his neighbor, or agrees to obey his superior. But it is extremely false in another sense, for the same man who cannot bear subordination or equality has so contemptible an opinion of himself that he thinks he was born only for vulgar pleasures. He readily settles for low desires, without daring to embark on lofty enterprises, of which he hardly dreams. So, far from thinking that humility ought to be preached to our contemporaries, I would have efforts made to give them a larger idea of themselves and of their kind. Humility is unhealthy for them. What they most lack, in my opinion, is pride. I would gladly trade several of our small virtues for this one vice.
